## From the PDE to the numerical solution

In the [periodic convection–diffusion example from Lecture 3](lecture_03.py#example-forward-euler-with-central-and-upwind-convection), both forward Euler schemes ran stably at $C=0.04$ and $D=0.016$, but upwind convection damped the wave more. When will perturbations grow, and how accurately does a stable scheme transport a wave? We will use the same model problem to answer both questions.

We write a homogeneous PDE as $L(\varphi)=0$. For one-dimensional convection–diffusion with constant velocity $v>0$ and diffusivity $\Gamma\geq 0$, the operator is

$$
L(\varphi)=\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial t}+v\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x}-\Gamma\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2}.
$$

We use a periodic spatial interval and prescribe the initial condition at $t^0=0$. On a uniform space–time mesh, $x_i=x_0+i\Delta x$ for $i=0,\ldots,N_x-1$ and $t^n=n\Delta t$ for $n=0,\ldots,N_t$. Spatial indices wrap periodically. Here $h=(\Delta x,\Delta t)$ denotes the discretization parameters.

With forward Euler in time and central differences for convection and diffusion, the discrete operator acting on a grid function $w$ is

$$
(L_h w)_i^n
=\frac{w_i^{n+1}-w_i^n}{\Delta t}
+v\frac{w_{i+1}^n-w_{i-1}^n}{2\Delta x}
-\Gamma\frac{w_{i+1}^n-2w_i^n+w_{i-1}^n}{\Delta x^2}.
$$

The PDE rows apply for $n=0,\ldots,N_t-1$. Together with the initial values they determine the grid function. Three objects enter the comparison:

- $\varphi(x,t)$ is the exact continuous solution.
- $\varphi_h=\{\varphi_i^n\}_{i,n}$ is the numerical solution, the grid function that solves $L_h(\varphi_h)=0$ with the prescribed discrete data, up to roundoff and solver error.
- $\pi_h\varphi=\{\varphi(x_i,t^n)\}_{i=0,\ldots,N_x-1;\ n=0,\ldots,N_t}$ is the projection of the exact solution onto this nodal grid, obtained by sampling it.

The **approximation error**, with numerical minus exact as our sign convention, is $e_h=\varphi_h-\pi_h\varphi$. In particular, $e_i^n=\varphi_i^n-\varphi(x_i,t^n)$.

![Conceptual sketch at one time level showing the exact curve, numerical nodal values, and the signed error at node i.](media/csc-error-light.svg){.light-content width=100%}
![Conceptual sketch at one time level showing the exact curve, numerical nodal values, and the signed error at node i.](media/csc-error-dark.svg){.dark-content width=100%}

### Error norms and residual

At a fixed time, the maximum norm records the largest nodal error and the mesh-weighted discrete two-norm measures the overall error across the interval:

$$
\|e^n\|_\infty=\max_i |e_i^n|,
\qquad
\|e^n\|_{2,h}=\left(\Delta x\sum_{i=0}^{N_x-1}|e_i^n|^2\right)^{1/2}.
$$

The subscript $h$ refers to the discretization parameters $h=(\Delta x,\Delta t)$. We measure the norm at a fixed time level $t^n$, so only the spatial spacing $\Delta x$ enters the sum. Each sample represents an interval of width $\Delta x$. If the nodal errors sample a continuous error profile $e(x,t^n)$, the squared discrete norm is a Riemann sum for the squared spatial $L^2$ norm.

$$
\Delta x\sum_{i=0}^{N_x-1}|e(x_i,t^n)|^2
\;\longrightarrow\;
\int_{x_0}^{x_0+L}|e(x,t^n)|^2\,\mathrm dx
\qquad\text{as }\Delta x\to 0,
$$

where $L=N_x\Delta x$ is the length of the periodic interval. For example, a constant unit error on an interval of length one gives a mesh-weighted norm of one for every $N_x$. The unweighted Euclidean norm gives $\sqrt{N_x}$ for the same profile.

Over the whole time interval we can use $\max_n\|e^n\|_\infty$ or $\max_n\|e^n\|_{2,h}$.

The norms tell us how far the numerical solution is from the exact samples. To see what error the stencil introduces in one step, we start with exact values and ask how closely they satisfy the discrete equation.

We use the Greek letter tau ($\tau$) for the **consistency residual**, also called the local truncation error in the derivative-scaled convention used here. On the mesh we write

$$
\tau_h=L_h(\pi_h\varphi).
$$

To evaluate it, we fill the stencil with exact solution samples at every required point and calculate how far the left-hand side of the discrete equation is from zero. Evaluating $L_h(\varphi_h)$ instead measures how closely the computed values satisfy the discrete equations. For this forward Euler stencil, $\Delta t\,\tau_i^n$ is the exact next value minus the result of one numerical step started from exact samples.

::: {.callout-note title="Consistency" icon=false}
A scheme is consistent if, for every sufficiently smooth exact solution $\varphi$ and each fixed final time $T$, its residual on the exact samples satisfies

$$
\max_{t^{n+1}\le T}\|\tau_h^n\|_{2,h}\longrightarrow 0
\qquad\text{as }\Delta x,\Delta t\to 0
$$

along the refinement family under consideration. The initial and boundary discretizations must also approximate their prescribed data consistently.
:::

We can check the residual directly by expanding the exact samples in Taylor series.


## Consistency of forward Euler with central differences

We Taylor-expand the exact samples about $(x_i,t^n)$. With all derivatives evaluated at this point, the three stencil errors are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\varphi(x_i,t^{n+1})-\varphi(x_i,t^n)}{\Delta t}-\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial t}
 &=\frac{\Delta t}{2}\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial t^2}+\frac{\Delta t^2}{6}\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial t^3}+\mathcal O(\Delta t^3),\\
\frac{\varphi(x_{i+1},t^n)-\varphi(x_{i-1},t^n)}{2\Delta x}-\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x}
 &=\frac{\Delta x^2}{6}\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x^3}+\mathcal O(\Delta x^4),\\
\frac{\varphi(x_{i+1},t^n)-2\varphi(x_i,t^n)+\varphi(x_{i-1},t^n)}{\Delta x^2}-\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2}
 &=\frac{\Delta x^2}{12}\frac{\partial^4\varphi}{\partial x^4}+\mathcal O(\Delta x^4).
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the forward Euler central operator $L_h$ and using $L(\varphi)=0$, we obtain

$$
\tau_i^n
=\frac{\Delta t}{2}\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial t^2}
+\Delta x^2\left(\frac{v}{6}\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x^3}-\frac{\Gamma}{12}\frac{\partial^4\varphi}{\partial x^4}\right)
+\mathcal O(\Delta t^2+\Delta x^4).
$$

The residual is $\mathcal O(\Delta t+\Delta x^2)$ for sufficiently smooth solutions. This gives first-order consistency in time and second-order consistency in space.

### Combining time and space errors

We now consider pure convection at constant velocity $v>0$. The PDE gives

$$
\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial t}=-v\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x}.
$$

For a smooth solution the spatial and temporal derivatives commute. Differentiating in time and substituting the PDE again gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial t^2}
&=-v\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial t}\right)
=v^2\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2},\\
\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial t^3}
&=v^2\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\left(\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial t}\right)
=-v^3\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x^3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the temporal contributions to the residual in terms of spatial derivatives and collect terms using the **Courant number** (often called the CFL number in this setting)

$$
C=\frac{v\Delta t}{\Delta x},
$$

the number of grid spacings traveled in one time step. At fixed $C$, keeping the second-order time contribution as well, we find

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{central}}
=\frac{v\Delta x}{2}C\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2}
+\frac{v\Delta x^2}{6}(1-C^2)\,\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x^3}
+\mathcal O(\Delta x^3).
$$

At $C=1$ the third-derivative contribution cancels. The term $\tfrac{v\Delta x}{2}\partial_x^2\varphi$ remains. Its coefficient is proportional to $\Delta x$, so the residual is still generally first order in $\Delta x$ along this fixed-$C$ refinement path. Here $\Delta t=\Delta x/v$, so the surviving term is also first order in $\Delta t$ along the same path. For upwind convection, the same Courant number has a stronger effect.

### Forward Euler with upwind convection

For $v>0$, the upstream node is $i-1$. We replace only the convection difference by $(w_i^n-w_{i-1}^n)/\Delta x$. Its error on the exact solution is $-\frac{\Delta x}{2}\partial_x^2\varphi+\frac{\Delta x^2}{6}\partial_x^3\varphi+\mathcal O(\Delta x^3)$. The time and diffusion expansions carry over, so the residual is generally $\mathcal O(\Delta t+\Delta x)$ for convection–diffusion. For pure convection and fixed $C$, it becomes

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{upwind}}
=\frac{v\Delta x}{2}(C-1)\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2}
+\frac{v\Delta x^2}{6}(1-C^2)\,\frac{\partial^3\varphi}{\partial x^3}
+\mathcal O(\Delta x^3).
$$

At $C=1$, the update becomes $\varphi_i^{n+1}=\varphi_{i-1}^n$. The exact pure-convection solution shifts by exactly one grid spacing in a step, so the numerical and exact nodal values agree in exact arithmetic.

## From Taylor expansion to Lax–Wendroff

The consistency analysis gives us a way to improve forward Euler with central convection. Forward Euler keeps only the term linear in $\Delta t$ in the Taylor expansion of the next value. The first term it leaves out is $\tfrac12\Delta t^2\partial_t^2\varphi$. Dividing by $\Delta t$ to form the residual gives the first-order time term we found above.

How can we include that missing term using only values we already have at $t^n$? For pure convection, the PDE relates the first time derivative to the spatial slope and the second time derivative to the spatial curvature, $\partial_t^2\varphi=v^2\partial_x^2\varphi$. So we can correct the forward Euler prediction by estimating the curvature at the current time. Keeping the quadratic term in the Taylor expansion gives

$$
\varphi(x_i,t^{n+1})=\varphi(x_i,t^n)
-v\Delta t\,\left.\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x}\right|_{(x_i,t^n)}
+\frac{v^2\Delta t^2}{2}\left.\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2}\right|_{(x_i,t^n)}
+\mathcal O(\Delta t^3).
$$

The central slope and compact central curvature both use the same three nodes $i-1$, $i$, and $i+1$. We therefore get the correction without an extra time level. The resulting **Lax–Wendroff** update is

$$
\varphi_i^{n+1}=\varphi_i^n
-\frac C2(\varphi_{i+1}^n-\varphi_{i-1}^n)
+\frac{C^2}{2}(\varphi_{i+1}^n-2\varphi_i^n+\varphi_{i-1}^n).
$$

The last term represents the second-order time contribution using neighboring values at the current time. Including it makes the derivative-scaled residual second order for smooth solutions under fixed-$C$ refinement. At $C=1$, the update again reduces to a shift by one node. The Taylor expansion gives the local residual. We now turn to what happens to perturbations over many time steps.

## From the Courant condition to stability

For pure convection, the characteristic through $(x_i,t^{n+1})$ meets the previous time level at $x_i-v\Delta t=x_i-C\Delta x$. That point is the exact one-step domain of dependence. The upwind stencil uses the two nodes $i-1$ and $i$, whose span contains the characteristic foot for $0\le C\le 1$. Repeating the stencil backward widens the numerical domain of dependence. Forward in time, a perturbation at $i$ can affect nodes $i$ and $i+1$ in one step. These are possible stencil connections, with zero weights at the endpoints $C=0$ or $C=1$.

![Conceptual space–time sketch comparing the upwind stencil with the characteristic foot for Courant numbers below and above one.](media/csc-characteristics-light.svg){.light-content width=100%}
![Conceptual space–time sketch comparing the upwind stencil with the characteristic foot for Courant numbers below and above one.](media/csc-characteristics-dark.svg){.dark-content width=100%}

For $C>1$ the characteristic foot lies outside the upwind stencil span. After $n$ steps, the stencil reaches at most $n\Delta x$ upstream, while the characteristic reaches $nC\Delta x$. At a fixed physical time $T=n\Delta t$, these distances are $vT/C$ and $vT$, respectively, measured along the periodically extended grid. Refining at fixed $C>1$ leaves the same gap. The geometric CFL condition $C\le 1$ lets the upwind stencil reach far enough upstream. How does exceeding this limit affect a small perturbation in the numerical solution?

### Watching a grid-scale perturbation grow

The animation starts with a periodic sine wave plus an alternating perturbation of amplitude $10^{-4}$. Both panels use forward Euler upwind on the same grid and show the same physical times. The exact reference is the transported smooth sine wave. What makes the small perturbation disappear at $C=0.8$ and become visible at $C=1.2$?

<video class="light-content" controls loop playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%" aria-label="Upwind comparison at Courant numbers 0.8 and 1.2"><source src="media/csc-upwind-light.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video>
<video class="dark-content" controls loop playsinline preload="metadata" width="100%" aria-label="Upwind comparison at Courant numbers 0.8 and 1.2"><source src="media/csc-upwind-dark.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video>

For a perturbation $z_i^n$, the linear upwind update is

$$
z_i^{n+1}=(1-C)z_i^n+Cz_{i-1}^n.
$$

On an even periodic grid, suppose $z_i^n=a^n(-1)^i$. The upstream sample has the opposite sign, so

$$
z_i^{n+1}=(1-2C)a^n(-1)^i.
$$

The factor $1-2C$ is the **gain** of this alternating mode. At $C=0.8$ it is $-0.6$, so the perturbation flips sign and shrinks in each step. At $C=1.2$ it is $-1.4$, so it flips sign and grows. At $C=1$ the profile shifts by one node, and the alternating mode flips sign with unchanged magnitude. For any initial profile, the update is a convex combination when $0\le C\le 1$, so its maximum norm cannot grow.

::: {.callout-note title="Stability" icon=false}
A linear one-step scheme is stable in a given norm if, for each fixed final time $T$, there is a constant $K_T$ independent of $h$ along the chosen refinement family such that every initial perturbation $z^0$ satisfies

$$
\|z^n\|\le K_T\|z^0\|
\qquad\text{for all }n\text{ with }t^n\le T
$$

when propagated by the numerical update.
:::

The convex-combination bound gives $K_T=1$ in the maximum norm for upwind convection when $0\le C\le 1$. A perturbation added during a step is subject to the same bound in subsequent steps.

The alternating pattern keeps its shape under the update. For a wave with a longer wavelength, a single time step can also shift the peaks by part of a wavelength. Complex numbers let us describe that shift and the change in amplitude with one multiplier.

## Complex numbers and phase

A complex number has Cartesian coordinates $a$ and $b$ in the complex plane. We write $z=a+\mathrm{i}b$, where $\mathrm{i}^2=-1$. The same number has polar coordinates $r=|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ and $\alpha=\arg(z)$, the angle measured counterclockwise from the positive real axis. We call $\alpha$ the **phase**. It is defined modulo $2\pi$ for $z\ne 0$.

![Cartesian and polar coordinates of a complex number and its reflection across the real axis.](media/csc-complex-plane-light.svg){.light-content width=100%}
![Cartesian and polar coordinates of a complex number and its reflection across the real axis.](media/csc-complex-plane-dark.svg){.dark-content width=100%}

Euler's formula $\exp(\mathrm{i}\alpha)=\cos(\alpha)+\mathrm{i}\sin(\alpha)$ gives $z=r\exp(\mathrm{i}\alpha)$. At $\alpha=\pi$ it gives Euler's identity $\exp(\mathrm{i}\pi)+1=0$. The **complex conjugate** is $\overline z=a-\mathrm{i}b=r\exp(-\mathrm{i}\alpha)$, so $z\overline z=a^2+b^2=|z|^2$. Multiplying two complex numbers multiplies their magnitudes and adds their phases. This makes a complex multiplier a convenient way to describe how a numerical time step changes both the amplitude and the position of a wave.

## Harmonic waves on a periodic grid

We consider $0\le x<L$ with periodic continuation, $\varphi(x+L,t)=\varphi(x,t)$. The node $x_{N_x}=L$ is identified with $x_0=0$, so there are $N_x$ distinct samples with $\Delta x=L/N_x$. We start with one real wave, $\cos(\kappa x)=\mathrm{Re}(\exp(\mathrm{i}\kappa x))$. The complex form lets us represent a spatial shift by multiplication. A Fourier representation of the continuous solution is

$$
\varphi(x,t)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}\widehat\varphi_m(t)\exp(\mathrm{i}\kappa_m x),
\qquad \kappa_m=\frac{2\pi m}{L}.
$$

Here $\widehat\varphi_m$ is the complex amplitude of mode $m$. For a real field, $\widehat\varphi_{-m}=\overline{\widehat\varphi_m}$. The **wavenumber** $\kappa_m$ describes the change in phase per unit length, and the **wavelength** is $\lambda_m=2\pi/|\kappa_m|$ for $m\ne 0$. Periodicity requires an integer number of cycles across the interval. The constant mode has $\kappa_0=0$. The smallest nonzero wavenumber magnitude is $2\pi/L$, corresponding to the longest wavelength $L$.

On the grid, modes whose indices differ by $N_x$ have identical samples. Indeed, the extra phase at node $x_j=j\Delta x$ is $2\pi j$. This indistinguishability is called **aliasing**. We use one representative per distinct grid mode. For even $N_x$, one choice is $m=-N_x/2+1,\ldots,N_x/2$. The largest magnitude is the **Nyquist wavenumber** $\kappa_{\max}=\pi/\Delta x$, with wavelength $2\Delta x$. Its samples alternate between $+1$ and $-1$, and the two signs of the Nyquist wavenumber give the same sampled mode. For odd $N_x$ the largest magnitude is $2\pi\lfloor N_x/2\rfloor/L$. We use even grids in the examples.

![Periodic mesh with the longest nonconstant mode and the alternating Nyquist mode.](media/csc-periodic-modes-light.svg){.light-content width=100%}
![Periodic mesh with the longest nonconstant mode and the alternating Nyquist mode.](media/csc-periodic-modes-dark.svg){.dark-content width=100%}

The open marker at $x=L$ repeats the sample at $x=0$. The dashed curves show the continuous cosines from which the filled markers were sampled.

Why work with waves? The PDE and the uniform periodic stencils are linear and have constant coefficients. Each wave evolves independently. In the continuous convection–diffusion equation, $\partial_x$ multiplies a mode by $\mathrm{i}\kappa$ and $\partial_x^2$ multiplies it by $-\kappa^2$. Thus its amplitude satisfies

$$
\frac{\mathrm d\widehat\varphi}{\mathrm dt}
=(-\mathrm{i}v\kappa-\Gamma\kappa^2)\widehat\varphi.
$$

Convection advances the wave by changing its phase. Diffusion reduces its magnitude, more rapidly at higher wavenumbers. We can compare the discrete evolution against both effects.

### Modified wavenumbers of spatial differences

We first keep time continuous. Let $w_j=\exp(\mathrm{i}\kappa x_j)$ and define $\theta=\kappa\Delta x$. At the neighboring nodes, $w_{j\pm1}=\exp(\mathrm{i}\kappa(x_j\pm\Delta x))=\exp(\pm\mathrm{i}\theta)w_j$. For the central first derivative $D^0$ and the backward (upwind for $v>0$) first derivative $D^-$, we define modified wavenumbers by $D^0 w=\mathrm{i}\widetilde\kappa_0 w$ and $D^-w=\mathrm{i}\widetilde\kappa_- w$. Substituting the shifted values gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{i}\widetilde\kappa_0
 &=\frac{\exp(\mathrm{i}\theta)-\exp(-\mathrm{i}\theta)}{2\Delta x},
&\widetilde\kappa_0&=\frac{\sin(\theta)}{\Delta x},\\
\mathrm{i}\widetilde\kappa_-
 &=\frac{1-\exp(-\mathrm{i}\theta)}{\Delta x},
&\widetilde\kappa_-&=\frac{\sin(\theta)-\mathrm{i}[1-\cos(\theta)]}{\Delta x}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For the compact central second derivative $D^-D^+$, we use $D^-D^+w=-\widetilde\kappa_2^2 w$ with the nonnegative magnitude

$$
\widetilde\kappa_2=\frac{2|\sin(\theta/2)|}{\Delta x}.
$$

![Real modified wavenumbers and the upwind imaginary contribution, normalized by the Nyquist wavenumber.](media/csc-modified-wavenumbers-light.svg){.light-content width=100%}
![Real modified wavenumbers and the upwind imaginary contribution, normalized by the Nyquist wavenumber.](media/csc-modified-wavenumbers-dark.svg){.dark-content width=100%}

The plot uses $0\le\kappa/\kappa_{\max}\le1$. For long waves, the real modified wavenumbers approach $\kappa$. For shorter waves, both first derivatives give the same smaller phase speed $v\sin(\theta)/\theta$. The central first derivative vanishes on the alternating mode because its two neighbors agree. Upwind adds a real decay rate $-v[1-\cos(\theta)]/\Delta x$ to the evolution, which damps short waves most strongly. The compact central second derivative continues to damp the alternating mode when $\Gamma>0$, with discrete decay rate $-\Gamma\widetilde\kappa_2^2$ of smaller magnitude than $-\Gamma\kappa^2$ at the same nonzero wavenumber.

## Von Neumann stability analysis

We now discretize both space and time. For one Fourier component we write $w_j^n=\widehat w^{\,n}\exp(\mathrm{i}j\theta)$ and substitute it into the update. The **gain function** (or amplification factor) $G(\theta)$ satisfies

$$
\widehat w^{\,n+1}=G(\theta)\widehat w^{\,n},
\qquad \widehat w^{\,n}=G(\theta)^n\widehat w^{\,0}.
$$

### One mode through one time step

For pure upwind convection, the shift by one node gives $G=(1-C)+C\exp(-\mathrm{i}\theta)$. Take $C=1/2$ and $\theta=\pi/2$, a wave with four nodes per wavelength. The gain is $G=(1-\mathrm{i})/2$, so its magnitude is $1/\sqrt{2}$ and its phase is $-\pi/4$. The exact wave moves to the right by half a grid spacing, which also gives a phase change of $-C\theta=-\pi/4$. The numerical step gets the phase right and reduces the amplitude, whereas the exact amplitude stays constant.

More generally, let $A_h$ be the spatial right-hand side after discretizing space, as in Lecture 3. If $A_hw=\lambda_h(\theta)w$ on a mode $w$, forward Euler applies $I+\Delta t\,A_h$ and gives $G(\theta)=1+\Delta t\,\lambda_h(\theta)$. The modified wavenumbers tell us how the spatial operator acts. The time update determines how that action becomes a gain.

### When the Fourier test applies

Here the PDE and numerical update are linear with constant coefficients on a uniform periodic grid. The same stencil acts at every node, including across the periodic boundary, so the one-step update is diagonal in the discrete Fourier basis. Each mode evolves independently. With fixed $\Delta t$ the same gain is applied at every step. Parseval's identity then makes $|G(\theta)|\le1$ for all represented modes equivalent to a nonincreasing discrete two-norm.

More generally, stability over $0\le t\le T$ requires a bound on $|G(\theta)|^n$ uniform in the modes and the refinement parameters for $n\Delta t\le T$. A bound $|G|\le1+K\Delta t$ with a uniform $K$ also suffices. The regions below describe non-amplification over the full range of Fourier angles. On an infinite uniform grid, Fourier analysis also applies to constant-coefficient stencils, with a continuous range of angles.

Variable coefficients, a nonuniform mesh, and nonperiodic boundary formulas can couple modes. A Fourier calculation for a constant-coefficient interior stencil can still help explain behavior in the interior, but the stability of the full problem then needs a separate argument. Energy estimates, maximum-norm bounds from convex combinations, and bounds on powers of the full update matrix are alternatives. For systems or multistep methods, a Fourier mode can carry several coupled amplitudes, so the corresponding test concerns powers of an amplification matrix.

### Forward Euler with central convection

With compact central diffusion, we use $D=\Gamma\Delta t/\Delta x^2$ and $C=v\Delta t/\Delta x$. Substitution gives

$$
G_{\mathrm{central}}(\theta)=1-4D\sin^2(\theta/2)-\mathrm{i}C\sin(\theta).
$$

Writing $s=\sin^2(\theta/2)$, we obtain

$$
|G_{\mathrm{central}}|^2-1
=4s\big[(C^2-2D)(1-s)+2D(2D-1)s\big].
$$

The expression inside brackets is linear in $s$. For $C,D\ge0$, requiring it to be nonpositive throughout $0<s\le1$ gives $C^2\le2D$ and $2D\le1$. The first restriction comes from the long-wave limit and the second from the alternating mode. On a particular finite grid, only the sampled angles enter the test. With $D=0$ and $C>0$, every mode with $\sin(\theta)\ne0$ grows per step.

### Forward Euler with upwind convection

For $v>0$, the gain is

$$
G_{\mathrm{upwind}}(\theta)
=1-C[1-\exp(-\mathrm{i}\theta)]-4D\sin^2(\theta/2)
=1-2(C+2D)\sin^2(\theta/2)-\mathrm{i}C\sin(\theta).
$$

At $\theta=\pi$, the condition $|G|\le1$ gives $C+2D\le1$. This also suffices for every angle: the update has weights $C+D$, $1-C-2D$, and $D$ on nodes $j-1$, $j$, and $j+1$. Under the bound all three are nonnegative and sum to one, so the gain, a weighted average of three unit-magnitude phase factors, has magnitude at most one.

![Non-amplification regions in Courant number and diffusion number for forward Euler with central or upwind convection.](media/csc-stability-regions-light.svg){.light-content width=100%}
![Non-amplification regions in Courant number and diffusion number for forward Euler with central or upwind convection.](media/csc-stability-regions-dark.svg){.dark-content width=100%}

Both schemes give $D\le1/2$ for pure diffusion. For pure convection, upwind allows $0\le C\le1$. If we refine with fixed positive $v$ and $\Gamma$, the two numbers are linked by $D/C=\Gamma/(v\Delta x)$. At a given mesh spacing, changing $\Delta t$ moves the operating point along this line through the origin. On fine meshes the diffusion restriction forces $\Delta t=\mathcal O(\Delta x^2)$ for these explicit schemes.

At the operating point from Lecture 3, $C^2=0.0016<2D=0.032<1$ and $C+2D=0.072<1$. Both updates are in their non-amplification regions. We still need to explain why their wave amplitudes differ.

### Lax–Wendroff for pure convection

The Lax–Wendroff update gives

$$
G_{\mathrm{LW}}(\theta)=1-\mathrm{i}C\sin(\theta)-2C^2\sin^2(\theta/2),
\qquad
|G_{\mathrm{LW}}(\theta)|^2=1-4C^2(1-C^2)\sin^4(\theta/2).
$$

For $0\le C\le1$, all modes have $|G_{\mathrm{LW}}|\le1$. For $C>1$, every nonconstant mode grows per step. At $C=1$, $G_{\mathrm{LW}}=\exp(-\mathrm{i}\theta)$, so every grid mode advances by exactly the right phase with unchanged magnitude. For $0<C<1$ and small $\theta$, the amplitude factor differs from one by $\mathcal O(\theta^4)$ and the phase error starts at order $\theta^3$. The Courant number affects both errors and also determines how many steps they accumulate over a given travel distance.

## Modified equations

The residual measures what the stencil does to the exact PDE solution. We can also ask what continuous equation a smooth interpolating field $\varphi_M$ must satisfy so that its samples approximately follow the numerical scheme. We Taylor-expand $L_h(\pi_h\varphi_M)=0$, use the original PDE to eliminate the time derivatives in the leading corrections, and keep terms to the desired order. This gives a **modified operator** $L_M$ such that $L_M(\varphi_M)=0$ to that order. The corrections enter with the opposite sign when moved to the right-hand side.

For the two forward Euler schemes, the leading convection and time corrections to the second derivative give

$$
\frac{\partial\varphi_M}{\partial t}+v\frac{\partial\varphi_M}{\partial x}
=\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\left(\Gamma-\frac{v\Delta x}{2}C\right)\frac{\partial^2\varphi_M}{\partial x^2}+\cdots,
 &\text{central convection},\\[6pt]
\displaystyle\left(\Gamma+\frac{v\Delta x}{2}(1-C)\right)\frac{\partial^2\varphi_M}{\partial x^2}+\cdots,
 &\text{upwind convection}.
\end{cases}
$$

The omitted terms include higher-order discretization terms. With physical diffusion present, the temporal correction also contains higher spatial derivatives, obtained by applying the full convection–diffusion operator twice. Central convection with forward Euler contributes negative numerical diffusivity. With physical diffusion present, the total coefficient can still be positive. In the pure-convection case, upwind convection with forward Euler adds diffusion for $0<C<1$, cancels it at $C=1$, and has negative numerical diffusivity for $C>1$. The modified equation describes the leading behavior for smooth, resolved fields. The exact update gives the growth rate of the grid-scale mode.

## Dissipation, amplitude, and phase errors

Over one time step, the exact gain of convection–diffusion is

$$
G_{\mathrm{exact}}(\theta)=\exp(-D\theta^2)\exp(-\mathrm{i}C\theta).
$$

We can compare a numerical gain $G$ to it in two ways:

- **Amplitude error.** The signed error per step in the amplitude factor is $|G|-\exp(-D\theta^2)$. A negative value means excess numerical damping, and a positive value means too little damping relative to the PDE. A **dissipation error** is an error in the decay rate. For $|G|>0$, the numerical rate is $-\log(|G|)/\Delta t$ and the physical rate is $\Gamma\kappa^2$. If $|G|>1$, the numerical amplitude grows. If $G=0$, the mode is removed in one step.
- **Phase error.** The phase increment differs from the exact value by $\arg(G)+C\theta$, modulo $2\pi$. To compare curves we follow the phase continuously from $\theta=0$ wherever $G\ne0$. Phase error means that a mode travels at the wrong speed. When the speed error varies with wavenumber, a combination of waves changes shape. This is **numerical dispersion**.

We can now explain the damping in Lecture 3. Its sine wave has one cycle on a 40-node mesh, so $\theta=2\pi/40$. Substituting the same $C$ and $D$ into the gains gives $|G_{\mathrm{exact}}|\approx0.999605$, $|G_{\mathrm{central}}|\approx0.999626$, and $|G_{\mathrm{upwind}}|\approx0.999133$. Central convection slightly underestimates the physical damping, while upwind overestimates it. The small difference per step compounds over the full run.

For pure convection at $C=0.6$, forward Euler with central differences amplifies intermediate wavenumbers. Upwind damps even long waves and strongly damps short waves. Lax–Wendroff has weaker damping for long waves and its phase lag varies with wavenumber. The sign convention in the phase plot is numerical minus exact, so a positive value means less phase advance to the right per step.

## Consistency order and convergence order

We return to the two errors defined at the start of the lecture. The **consistency error** $\tau_h=L_h(\pi_h\varphi)$ is the residual of exact samples in the discrete equations. The **consistency order** describes how fast it tends to zero for smooth solutions. For example, a bound

$$
\max_{t^n<T}\|\tau_h^n\|_{2,h}
\le K(\Delta t^p+\Delta x^q)
$$

gives at least order $p$ in time and $q$ in space for the derivative-scaled residual. Forward Euler with central convection and diffusion gives $p=1$ and $q=2$. If we start a step with exact data, the one-step solution defect contains an additional factor of $\Delta t$.

::: {.callout-note title="Convergence" icon=false}
A scheme converges in the mesh-weighted two-norm if, for each fixed final time $T$ and admissible initial datum, its global solution error satisfies

$$
E_h=\max_{t^n\le T}\|\varphi_h^n-(\pi_h\varphi)^n\|_{2,h}
\longrightarrow 0
\qquad\text{as }\Delta x,\Delta t\to 0
$$

along the chosen refinement family.
:::

The convergence order describes how fast $E_h$ decreases along that refinement path.

Let $B_h$ be the one-step update matrix. The numerical state satisfies $\varphi_h^{n+1}=B_h\varphi_h^n$. If we start the step with exact samples, the result differs from the next exact sample by the one-step defect. With our residual convention this gives $(\pi_h\varphi)^{n+1}=B_h(\pi_h\varphi)^n+\Delta t\,\tau_h^n$. Subtracting the two equations and applying the recurrence repeatedly gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
e^{n+1}&=B_he^n-\Delta t\,\tau_h^n,\\
e^n&=B_h^n e^0-\Delta t\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}B_h^{n-1-m}\tau_h^m.
\end{aligned}
$$

Each step propagates the old error and injects a new defect. Stability gives a uniform bound $\|B_h^k\|_{2,h}\le K_T$ for $k\Delta t\le T$, where the matrix norm is induced by the mesh-weighted two-norm. Applying it to the recurrence and using $n\Delta t\le T$ gives

$$
E_h\le K_T\left(\|e^0\|_{2,h}+T\max_{t^n<T}\|\tau_h^n\|_{2,h}\right).
$$

With exact initial samples and a uniform stability bound, the global error inherits the residual's order bound. The observed order along a refinement path depends on how $\Delta t$ changes with $\Delta x$. For example, for forward Euler with central differences and fixed positive $\Gamma$, taking $\Delta t$ proportional to $\Delta x^2$ within the stable region makes both terms in $\mathcal O(\Delta t+\Delta x^2)$ of order $\Delta x^2$. Measuring second order along this path is compatible with first-order time consistency.

In a grid refinement study we can estimate the observed order from $\log(E_{\mathrm{coarse}}/E_{\mathrm{fine}})/\log(r)$, where $r=\Delta x_{\mathrm{coarse}}/\Delta x_{\mathrm{fine}}$. We keep the physical problem, comparison time, norm, and refinement rule fixed. A rate derived for smooth solutions need not hold for the rectangular pulse.

### The Lax–Richtmyer equivalence theorem

::: {.callout-note title="Lax–Richtmyer equivalence theorem" icon=false}
For a well-posed linear initial-value problem and a consistent linear finite difference approximation, stability is equivalent to convergence for all admissible initial data. Both statements concern a fixed time interval and the same refinement family.
:::

The proof sketch below uses the one-step setting of this lecture.

**Stability implies convergence.** For smooth initial data, consistency makes the residual tend to zero. The error recurrence and uniform bound on powers of $B_h$ then make the global error tend to zero, provided the initial discretization error also vanishes. To extend this to rougher data, we approximate them by smooth data. Well-posedness bounds the effect of that replacement in the exact evolution. Stability and a uniformly bounded transfer of initial data to the grid bound it in the numerical evolution. Since smooth data are dense in the solution space, the replacement error can be made arbitrarily small.

**Convergence implies stability.** Think of the numerical evolution operators $B_h^nP_h$ as acting on one complete space of initial data, where $P_h$ transfers continuous data to the grid. Convergence on the fixed interval for each initial datum means that the numerical evolutions are bounded for that datum. The uniform boundedness principle upgrades these datum-by-datum bounds to one operator bound independent of the datum, $h$, and $n$ with $n\Delta t\le T$. This controls $B_h^n$ itself when grid data can be lifted back to the continuous space with uniformly bounded norm. For example, on our periodic grid in $L^2$, $P_h$ can first project onto the retained Fourier modes and then sample that trigonometric polynomial. The lift reconstructs the polynomial from its grid values. With one Fourier representative per grid mode, Parseval's identity equates the continuous norm of the lift with the mesh-weighted grid norm. This argument uses convergence for all initial data. A refinement study for one sine wave tests only that wave.
